periods.activity_title: Our Address on a Borderless Planet
periods.textbook_anchor: The Blue Planet — Students fill in their full layered address from name through to planet (p. 162)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla's reflection that Earth looks borderless from space, then invites students to share what they think the planet might look like from very far away. The teacher points out that from space no country boundaries are visible — only land and ocean. Students share one idea each about what 'borderless' means to them.

Students open Textbook p. 162 and fill in their own layered address — name, house number or building name, street name, village or town or city, district, state or Union Territory, country, planet. After completing the address, pairs compare their entries and note which layers they share and which differ. The teacher guides a brief class discussion: what does adding 'Planet: Earth' at the end of an address tell us?

With the globe on the teacher's desk, students gather round and take turns locating India. The teacher draws attention to the oceans and asks whether they appear connected or separate. Students trace ocean boundaries with a finger and share what they notice, connecting this to the idea that nature does not divide the world the way maps do. The teacher introduces Wing Commander Rakesh Sharma's reply 'Saare Jahaan Se Achcha' from the 'Do you know?' box and asks what feeling that answer carries.

Students write one sentence in their notebooks completing the prompt: 'Earth is our shared home because ___.' Two or three volunteers share aloud. The teacher closes by naming the chapter's central idea — that air, water, animals, seeds, people, and ideas all move freely across the world, making Earth a place we all belong to together.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain, using a layered address and a globe, how human-made boundaries differ from the natural, borderless character of Earth.
periods.section_context: Layered personal address (name through planet), globe exploration of connected oceans and India's location, Shubhanshu Shukla's borderless-Earth reflection, Rakesh Sharma's 'Saare Jahaan Se Achcha', DIGIPIN digital address system.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you were floating in space looking down, how would you know where one country ends and another begins?' Let students grapple with the idea that the answer is — you wouldn't. Invite students whose families have moved cities or states to share how their address changed, reinforcing that boundaries are human agreements, not natural lines.

periods.textbook_anchor: Story 1: The Travelling Birds! — Students trace rosy starling migration from Russia and Mongolia to India on a globe using a string (p. 165)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the rosy starling story from Textbook p. 164 aloud, pausing to ask: where do these birds come from, what do they eat, and why do farmers welcome them? Students identify Russia and Mongolia on the globe before the activity begins. The teacher confirms that locust-eating birds provide a natural service to farmers — no spraying required.

In small groups, students open Textbook p. 165 and use a length of coloured string to trace the rosy starling's route from Russia or Mongolia down to India on the globe. Each group decides the most likely path the birds would take over land. Groups record in their notebooks: the countries or regions the string passes through, and one natural feature (sea, mountain range, or river) that the birds must cross. Groups share their traced routes with the class and compare any differences.

Students respond in their notebooks to the two write tasks from Textbook p. 164: whether the rosy starling visits their area and what it might be called locally, and what the story tells us about nature. The teacher encourages students to draw on what the globe trace showed them — the bird crosses many countries without a passport or permission.

A brief whole-class share: the teacher asks two or three groups to read their 'what this story tells us about nature' sentences. The teacher names the key idea — migratory birds are living proof that nature moves freely across the world — and connects this back to the borderless view from space discussed when filling in addresses.

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace the route of a migratory animal on a globe and record natural features crossed, demonstrating that living things move across geographic boundaries.
periods.section_context: Rosy starlings, migration from Russia and Mongolia to India, locust and grasshopper feeding, globe string trace of migration route, local name inquiry.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt groups: 'Did your string go over a sea or an ocean? How do you think the birds manage that?' Students from different regions may know local names for winter birds — invite them to share, reinforcing that regional variation in naming is perfectly valid here.

periods.textbook_anchor: Story 1: The Travelling Birds! — Students write a short postcard imagining they are a bird travelling the world, describing what they see and what helps on the journey (p. 165)
materials: blank postcard-sized card or notebook page

time_bands.activity: The teacher reminds students of the rosy starling's journey traced on the globe and asks: what might a bird notice as it flies over mountains, seas, and different lands? Students brainstorm orally — wind currents, warm weather, food along the way, lights of cities at night. The teacher writes helpful vocabulary on the board: ocean currents, warm climate, flock, route.

Students open Textbook p. 165 and write a short postcard or note imagining they are a bird on a long migration. The postcard must mention at least one thing they see on the journey and at least one natural helper — wind, ocean currents, or warm weather. Students are free to draw a small picture on the 'stamp' corner of their card. The teacher circulates and encourages students to use first-person voice and to name at least one place from the globe trace.

Volunteers share their postcards aloud. The class listens and notes: did the writer mention a natural helper? Did they name a place from the migration route? After two or three readings, the teacher highlights how each postcard — even though imaginary — is grounded in real natural phenomena that allow birds to travel thousands of kilometres.
Students write one closing sentence in their notebooks: 'One thing that helps a migratory bird on its journey is ___.' This anchors the creative work back to factual recall.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express, through a creative first-person account, the natural forces that enable long-distance migration, connecting imaginative writing to observed phenomena.
periods.section_context: Rosy starling migration, wind currents, ocean currents, warm weather as journey helpers, postcard format creative writing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What feeling do you think the bird has when it finally sees India's warm fields after months of flying?' This helps students move beyond facts into empathy with the natural world — a disposition the chapter builds toward. Students who prefer drawing may submit a picture-postcard with a caption.

periods.activity_title: Yoga Travels the World — Discussion and Pose Exploration
periods.section_ref: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World! — Students discuss why yoga became popular in so many countries (p. 167)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the yoga section from the textbook aloud and pauses to establish three facts with the class: yoga is at least 3,000 years old, it began in India, and the UN recognised 21 June as the International Day of Yoga. The teacher asks students to raise their hand if they or someone at home has practised yoga, building a personal connection to the global story.

Students open Textbook p. 167 and discuss in pairs: why do they think yoga became popular in so many countries? After pair talk, the class shares ideas and the teacher lists reasons on the board — health benefits, peace of mind, no equipment needed, harmony with nature, travellers spreading the practice. The teacher connects this to the chapter's theme: just as birds and plants cross borders, so do ideas and practices.

Students respond in writing to the second task from Textbook p. 167: name a yoga pose they have tried or seen, and say what they think it helps with. Students who have not tried yoga are invited to describe one they have seen in pictures or TV. After writing, three or four students share their responses. The teacher weaves in the idea that when a practice rooted in harmony with nature spreads globally, it becomes part of everyone's shared heritage.

The teacher poses a closing question for students to answer in one sentence in their notebooks: 'How is the spread of yoga similar to the rosy starling's journey?' This comparison sharpens the chapter's unifying idea — things of value cross borders naturally.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how a cultural practice rooted in one country can travel globally and describe the reasons for its wide acceptance.
periods.section_context: Yoga's 3,000-year history in India, spread through travellers and scholars, UN International Day of Yoga on 21 June, yoga poses and their benefits, harmony with nature and self.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If yoga had stayed only in India, what might the world have missed?' This moves students from recall to evaluation of cultural sharing. Invite students whose families practise yoga or another traditional movement form to share briefly — this surfaces diverse regional traditions without labelling them.

periods.activity_title: Chilli's Globe Journey and the Story of a Travelling Food
periods.section_ref: Story 3: Chilli—A Spice that Changed our Lives!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 3: Chilli—A Spice that Changed our Lives! — Students trace the journey of chillies from South America to India on a globe using a coloured string (p. 168)
materials: coloured string (different colour from earlier use)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a quick show-of-hands question: who had something spicy for breakfast or dinner yesterday? Then asks: where do students think the spice came from originally? After hearing guesses, the teacher reads the chilli story from Textbook p. 168. Students identify South America and India on the globe before the string-trace activity begins.

In pairs, students open Textbook p. 168 and use a coloured string to trace the chilli's journey from South America to India on the globe, following Portuguese trading routes around the southern tip of Africa or across the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. Each pair records in their notebooks: the approximate route their string took, the oceans crossed, and one question the journey raises — for example, how long might such a voyage have taken, or who carried the chilli seeds.

Students respond to the two write tasks from Textbook p. 168: what would happen if chillies disappeared from their kitchen for a week, and a recipe from home where black pepper is used instead of red chilli. Students who already know such a recipe write it down; those who do not make a reasonable guess and note to check at home. The teacher reminds the class that before chillies arrived, black pepper was the main spice — this helps students appreciate how food habits can change over centuries.

Two or three pairs share their globe-trace route and the question they recorded. The teacher highlights that the same ship that brought chillies may have carried other plants too — potatoes, tomatoes, peanuts — and students are invited to briefly name any food they now know came from elsewhere. This plants the idea for the food-travel research task from Textbook p. 168 that students can pursue as an independent inquiry.

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace a plant's intercontinental journey on a globe and identify how its arrival changed food practices in a new region.
periods.section_context: Chilli originating in South America, Portuguese traders bringing it to India 400–500 years ago, black pepper as earlier spice, globe string trace of chilli's journey, kitchen impact of chilli disappearing, recipes using black pepper.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask pairs: 'Why do you think the chilli found such a welcome home in India?' Encourage students to think about climate, soil, and taste preferences. Students whose families use black pepper in specific regional recipes (pepper rasam, pepper chicken, etc.) should be encouraged to share — regional food diversity is the point here.

periods.activity_title: Sweet Journeys and Flower Festivals — Sugar and Marigold Stories
periods.section_ref: Story 4: The Sweet Story of Sugar! / Story 5: The Mexican Marigold Moves into India!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 5: The Mexican Marigold Moves into India! — Students write why both Indian and Mexican cultures use marigolds during their festivals (p. 170)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads Story 4 aloud from Textbook p. 169. Students note three items that India sent to the world (jaggery and sugar, rice, mangoes, bananas) and one item that came to India from China (paper). The class discusses the two prompt questions from p. 169 in a quick open round: which one Indian food would they share with the world, and what new food items might travel in the future?

The teacher reads Story 5 from Textbook pp. 170–171. Students note where marigolds originated and where they are now deeply embedded. Discussion question: why do they think a flower from Mexico became inseparable from Indian temples, weddings, and Diwali? Students share in pairs, then report back. The teacher draws out the idea that colour, fragrance, and the human love of beauty in celebration are universal — making it easy for cultural elements to cross borders.

Students open Textbook p. 170 and write their response to the first write task: why do they think both Indian and Mexican cultures use marigolds during their festivals? Students then write their response to the second write task from p. 171: why do people in different countries include flowers in their celebrations? Students aim for two or three sentences per response, grounding their answer in the chapter's examples.

Three or four students share their marigold-festival responses. The teacher draws a simple two-column note on the board — 'Marigold in Mexico' and 'Marigold in India' — and students contribute one detail each. The teacher closes by naming the pattern: foods, flowers, and ideas that resonate with universal human feelings travel the furthest and stay the longest.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare how a single natural element is adopted into different cultural celebrations and explain why shared human values enable cross-cultural exchange.
periods.section_context: India's jaggery and sugar production and spread, rice, mangoes, bananas travelling from India, paper from China, marigold origins in Mexico, marigold use in Indian temples and festivals, Indian and Mexican festival use of marigolds.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Think of one flower or food used in a festival in your family — do you know where it originally came from?' Students from different states often have different festival flowers or sweets; this surfaces regional variety without requiring prior research.

periods.activity_title: Indian Cows in Brazil — Animals that Crossed Continents
periods.section_ref: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil!
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil! — Students find out the names of at least five different breeds of cows with teacher or elder help (p. 172)
materials: reference books or printed breed-name list if available

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads Story 6 from Textbook p. 171 aloud. Students identify the three Indian cow breeds named (Gir, Kankrej, Ongole), the country they travelled to (Brazil), and the surprising fact that these breeds appear on Brazilian stamps and coins. The teacher asks: why would a country put a foreign cow breed on its money?

Students open Textbook p. 172 and begin the inquiry task: with the teacher's help, they find the names of at least five different breeds of cows. The teacher writes the three named in the story on the board as a starting point and prompts students to think of breeds they may have heard of at home, from elders, or from rural visits — for example, Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Tharparkar, or locally known breeds. Students record all names they gather in their notebooks with any one known feature of each breed.

Students write a short response to the first write task from Textbook p. 171: what does this story tell us about animals moving from one place to another? Students should connect this to earlier stories — just as plants and birds crossed borders, animals did too, and they brought lasting benefit to the places they went.

Students share their breed lists with a partner and compare: did they find the same five, or different ones? The class pool is collected on the board to build a class list of breeds. The teacher closes by asking: 'What does it mean for Brazil that these Indian breeds now supply most of its milk?' — drawing out the idea of lasting global contribution.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a guided inquiry to identify and record multiple varieties of a domesticated animal and explain how animal movement across regions creates lasting benefits.
periods.section_context: Gir, Kankrej, and Ongole Indian cow breeds, Portuguese traders taking cows to Brazil, Brazilian dairy supply, cows on Brazilian stamps and coins, cow breed inquiry (Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Tharparkar, and others).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you were a farmer in Brazil 300 years ago and these cows arrived, what difference would you notice first?' This grounds the global story in a concrete, local-scale imagining. Students from farming families or rural backgrounds may already know breed names — invite them to take the lead in building the class list.

periods.activity_title: Things Around Us That Travelled — A Classroom Inventory
periods.section_ref: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil! / Web of Life
periods.textbook_anchor: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil! — Students list things in their house or school that may have come from another part of the world and find out their origins (p. 172)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a quick look around the classroom: what objects in this room might have origins in another country or continent? Students call out ideas freely — the cotton in their uniform, the rubber eraser, the paper in their books. The teacher notes that almost everything has travelled, connecting this to Story 6's lesson that animals, like plants and ideas, cross borders.

Students open Textbook p. 172 and use the five category prompts — clothing, food, sports, musical instruments, tree — to make their own list of things at home or school that may have come from another part of the world. For each item, students record what they think its origin might be. Students work individually, then share with a partner to add items they missed.

The teacher reads the Web of Life section from Textbook p. 173 aloud. Students listen for the synthesising idea: whether a bird migrates, a seed grows in new soil, or yoga reaches every corner of the globe, it all shows that we are connected. Students then add one sentence to their notebook list: 'The item I am most surprised about is ___ because I thought it came from ___.' The teacher asks two or three students to share their surprise item.

Brief class share and closing reflection: the teacher draws out the chapter's web metaphor — each item on students' lists is one thread. The teacher names the idea that caring for each other and the planet means recognising these threads of connection, not cutting them.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe everyday objects in their immediate environment and identify their global origins, demonstrating that daily life is shaped by cross-continental exchange.
periods.section_context: Classroom and household objects with global origins (clothing, food, sports equipment, musical instruments, trees), five category inventory from textbook, Web of Life synthesis of bird, plant, and idea migration.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which item on your list surprised you the most — something you thought was completely Indian but actually came from elsewhere?' This question drives genuine inquiry and helps students see the Web of Life idea as personally relevant. Students from different states often have different items on their list; all lists are equally valid.

periods.activity_title: Two-String World Map — Tracing What Came and What Went
periods.textbook_anchor: Web of Life — Students list things that came to India from other countries and those that travelled from India to the world, then trace their journeys on a map using two different coloured strings (p. 173)
materials: globe or large outline world map
two colours of string or wool
periods.visual_aids: Globe or large outline world map

time_bands.activity: The teacher revisits the chapter's stories quickly by asking students to name one thing that came to India from elsewhere (chilli, marigold, paper) and one thing that went from India to the world (yoga, jaggery and sugar, Indian cow breeds, rice, mangoes). Students contribute from memory. The teacher introduces the two-string map task from Textbook p. 173 as a way to see all these journeys at once on a single globe or map.

In groups of three or four, students open Textbook p. 173 and build two lists in their notebooks: things that came to India from other countries (chilli from South America, marigold from Mexico, paper from China, rosy starlings from Russia and Mongolia) and things that went from India to the world (yoga, sugar and jaggery, rice, mangoes, bananas, Gir and Kankrej and Ongole cow breeds). Groups then use two different colours of string on the globe or map — one colour for arrivals, one for departures — and trace as many journeys as they can. Each group records which journeys their strings represented.

Groups report back: what was the longest journey their string traced? Which direction had more threads — arrivals to India or departures from India? The teacher uses this to surface the idea that exchange flows in both directions, making every place both a giver and a receiver — the essence of the Web of Life.

Each student writes one closing sentence: 'The journey I found most interesting was ___ because ___.' The teacher names the Web of Life idea one final time: every thread on the map is also a thread of human connection.

periods.implied_lo: Students can organise information about intercontinental exchanges into a two-directional map, distinguishing what arrived in a region from what departed, and draw conclusions about global interconnection.
periods.section_context: Two-string globe or map trace of arrivals to India (chilli, marigold, paper, rosy starlings) and departures from India (yoga, sugar and jaggery, rice, mangoes, bananas, Gir, Kankrej, Ongole cow breeds), Web of Life synthesis.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'Looking at your two strings together, what does the pattern tell you about India's place in the world?' This pushes students from listing to analysis. Groups that finish quickly can add the rosy starling migration route as a third trace in a neutral colour, showing that nature's journeys overlap with human ones.

periods.activity_title: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam — We Are One Family
periods.textbook_anchor: One Earth, One Family! — Students write what 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' teaches us and one way they can care for the Earth (p. 176)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the 'One Earth, One Family!' section from Textbook p. 176 aloud, pausing on the phrase 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' and asking students to repeat it softly. The teacher explains that this ancient Indian idea extends family membership to all people, animals, trees, rivers, air, and sky. Students are invited to share in one word how this idea makes them feel.

Students open Textbook p. 176 and complete the three write tasks: what 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' teaches us; the meaning in their own words; and how we can live like one big family even when we are different. The teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with: 'Think of one time you helped or shared with someone who was very different from you — that is already living this idea.'

Students write responses to the two 'Let us reflect' tasks from Textbook p. 176: one way they can care for the Earth, and one thing from India they think could travel to other parts of the world. The teacher connects the second task back to all the chapter's stories — yoga, jaggery, rice — and affirms that students' own suggestions are a continuation of that long tradition of sharing.

Volunteers share their 'one way to care for the Earth' responses. The teacher collects them on the board — planting a tree, saving water, not wasting food — and names this as the chapter's invitation: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam is not just a phrase but a way of acting. Students leave having written at least one concrete action they commit to, grounded in the chapter's central value.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate the meaning of a core social-ethical value in their own words and identify at least one concrete personal action that expresses care for the shared Earth.
periods.section_context: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (the world is one family), Earth as the only known planet with life, MoEFCC logo as symbol of nature-human balance, writing meaning in own words, living as one family despite differences, one way to care for the Earth, one item from India to share with the world.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If every person in your class did one thing on the board to care for the Earth, what would your school look like in one month?' This makes the abstract value of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam tangible and local. Students who wish to express their commitment through a drawing or a short poem instead of prose should be welcomed — the disposition matters more than the format.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: In groups, students build two lists of intercontinental exchanges and use two colours of string on a globe or map to trace arrivals to and departures from India, then report on direction, distance, and what the pattern reveals.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can articulate the meaning of a core social-ethical value in their own words and identify at least one concrete personal action that expresses care for the shared Earth.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (the world is one family), Earth as the only known planet with life, MoEFCC logo as symbol of nature-human balance, writing meaning in own words, living as one family despite differences, one way to care for the Earth, one item from India to share with the world.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: One Earth, One Family! — Students write what 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' teaches us and one way they can care for the Earth (p. 176)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students read the Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam section, write its meaning in their own words and how to live as one family, then name one concrete personal action to care for the Earth and one Indian thing they would share with the world.

assessment_items.question_text: Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla noticed that Earth looks borderless from space. Which of the following best explains why national borders are not visible from space?

options.label: A
options.text: National borders are human-made agreements, not physical features of the Earth.

options.label: B
options.text: National borders are natural lines formed by rivers and mountains.

options.label: C
options.text: National borders are too small to be seen from any distance.

options.label: D
options.text: National borders were removed when space travel began.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item checks whether students grasped the chapter's foundational idea that borders are human constructs, not natural features.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain, using a layered address and a globe, how human-made boundaries differ from the natural, borderless character of Earth.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses natural geographic features (rivers, mountains) with political borders — a common conflation when maps show rivers as boundary markers.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student thinks the issue is scale rather than nature — they have not grasped that borders are human constructs with no physical form at any scale.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has invented a reason not found in the chapter, suggesting they did not engage with the borderless-Earth concept and are guessing.

assessment_items.question_text: Rosy starlings travel from Russia and Mongolia to India every winter. Using what you traced on the globe, describe the journey: name one natural feature (such as a sea, mountain range, or large land area) the birds cross, and explain one way the natural world helps them make this long journey.
expected_elements: Names at least one natural feature crossed on the migration route (e.g., a sea, a mountain range, or a large land mass between Russia or Mongolia and India).
Identifies at least one natural helper that enables the journey (wind currents, warm weather at the destination, or availability of food such as locusts and grasshoppers in India).
Connects the journey to the idea that nature moves freely across borders.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any geographically reasonable natural feature for the migration route — the Himalayas, the Caspian Sea, the central Asian steppe, or the Indian Ocean coast are all valid. Regional variation in named features is expected and acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace the route of a migratory animal on a globe and record natural features crossed, demonstrating that living things move across geographic boundaries.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

expected_elements: Names at least one natural feature crossed on the migration route (e.g., a sea, a mountain range, or a large land mass between Russia or Mongolia and India).
Identifies at least one natural helper that enables the journey (wind currents, warm weather at the destination, or availability of food such as locusts and grasshoppers in India).
Connects the journey to the idea that nature moves freely across borders.

assessment_items.task: You are a rosy starling flying from Russia to India for the winter. Write a short postcard (four to six sentences) to a friend back home. Tell your friend: one thing you see or feel on the long journey, and one thing that helps you travel so far. You may also draw a small picture on your postcard.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My postcard:
Dear friend,
I have been flying for many days now. Today I crossed ___ (name a place or natural feature). It was ___ (describe what you saw or felt). What really helped me on this journey was ___ (name a natural helper). India is ___ (one thing about your arrival). Wish you were here!
Your friend, Rosy
format_of_output: Written postcard of four to six sentences following the scaffold
Optional small drawing in the stamp corner
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether the student names a real natural feature or helper from the chapter (wind, warm weather, food availability) even if the creative details are imaginative. Accept any geographically reasonable place name for the route.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express, through a creative first-person account, the natural forces that enable long-distance migration, connecting imaginative writing to observed phenomena.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can blend factual knowledge about natural migration helpers with first-person creative expression, showing that the scientific idea (wind, warm weather, food) was internalised rather than merely memorised.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts four slots: a natural feature or place crossed, a feeling or observation, a natural helper, and an impression of India on arrival. A strong response fills all four with chapter-accurate content; a weak response fills slots with vague or invented details unconnected to the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a real natural feature (a sea, mountain range, or steppe), correctly identifies a natural helper (warm winds, food abundance), and the arrival description connects to India's warm climate or farmland. Weak: uses only generic phrases ('it was a long journey', 'many things helped me') with no chapter-specific content.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who prefer drawing may submit a picture-postcard where the image communicates the journey and a two-sentence caption names the natural helper — this demonstrates the same outcome through a different mode.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The postcard format matches the textbook task exactly and gives a concise, bounded creative frame that keeps the writing grounded in the specific migration story rather than becoming open-ended.

assessment_items.question_text: Yoga began in India more than 3,000 years ago and is now practised in almost every country. Give two reasons why you think yoga spread so widely across the world.
expected_elements: Identifies at least one practical reason for yoga's spread (e.g., it benefits health, promotes mental peace, requires no special equipment, is accessible to all).
Identifies at least one reason related to how it spread (e.g., travellers, scholars, or teachers from India introduced it to other countries).
Connects yoga's global reach to the broader idea that valuable cultural practices cross borders naturally.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept two distinct and plausible reasons even if they do not exactly match the textbook — the item assesses reasoning, not recall of specific sentences.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 2: Yoga—India's Gift to the World!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how a cultural practice rooted in one country can travel globally and describe the reasons for its wide acceptance.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

expected_elements: Identifies at least one practical reason for yoga's spread (e.g., it benefits health, promotes mental peace, requires no special equipment, is accessible to all).
Identifies at least one reason related to how it spread (e.g., travellers, scholars, or teachers from India introduced it to other countries).
Connects yoga's global reach to the broader idea that valuable cultural practices cross borders naturally.

assessment_items.question_text: The chilli plant originally came from South America and was brought to India about 400 to 500 years ago. Before chillies arrived, which spice did Indians mainly use to make food spicy?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This tests direct recall from the chilli story and checks whether students read the section carefully enough to note that black pepper was the earlier spice of heat.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 3: Chilli—A Spice that Changed our Lives!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace a plant's intercontinental journey on a globe and identify how its arrival changed food practices in a new region.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses turmeric (used for colour and health) with the spice used for heat — a reasonable confusion but not supported by the chapter's specific statement.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student names a common Indian spice but has not retained the chapter's specific claim that black pepper was the heat spice before chillies arrived.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student names another common Indian spice without connecting it to the specific function (heat/spiciness) the chapter highlighted.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter tells us that the marigold flower came from Mexico but has become deeply part of Indian culture — seen at temples, weddings, and festivals. People in both Mexico and India use marigolds in their celebrations. Why do you think a flower from so far away became so important in Indian life? Use what you have read about sugar, yoga, and the marigold to explain your answer.
look_for: Identifies a specific quality of the marigold (bright colour, fragrance, beauty) that resonated with Indian values of warmth and celebration.
Connects the marigold's journey to the broader pattern of things travelling and finding a welcome home in new cultures (as with yoga, sugar, or chilli).
Notes that both Indian and Mexican cultures share a universal human practice of using flowers in celebration — making the exchange natural.
Attempts to reason about why some elements from distant cultures become permanent parts of a new culture while others do not.
assessment_items.annotation: Look for reasoning that goes beyond 'because it is beautiful' to include the cultural resonance idea (warmth, spirituality, celebration) and the cross-cultural pattern the chapter establishes. Reward students who draw a comparison to another chapter story.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 5: The Mexican Marigold Moves into India!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare how a single natural element is adopted into different cultural celebrations and explain why shared human values enable cross-cultural exchange.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: Identifies a specific quality of the marigold (bright colour, fragrance, beauty) that resonated with Indian values of warmth and celebration.
Connects the marigold's journey to the broader pattern of things travelling and finding a welcome home in new cultures (as with yoga, sugar, or chilli).
Notes that both Indian and Mexican cultures share a universal human practice of using flowers in celebration — making the exchange natural.
Attempts to reason about why some elements from distant cultures become permanent parts of a new culture while others do not.

assessment_items.question_text: Indian cow breeds such as the Gir, Kankrej, and Ongole were taken to Brazil by Portuguese traders. These breeds now supply more than three-fourths of Brazil's milk, and appear on Brazilian stamps and coins. Name two other cow breeds (not from this story) and explain what the story of Indian cows in Brazil tells us about how animals can help connect different parts of the world.
expected_elements: Names at least two cow breeds not mentioned in the story (e.g., Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Tharparkar, or any other valid breed identified during the inquiry activity).
States clearly that animals, like plants and ideas, can cross continents and bring lasting benefit to new places.
Makes a connection to the chapter's broader theme — that trade and travel move not just goods but living beings that become part of other societies.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any verifiable Indian cow breed name for the inquiry part. The explanation of connection is the primary assessment target — the breed names demonstrate the inquiry was conducted. Regional variation in breed names is expected and acceptable.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a guided inquiry to identify and record multiple varieties of a domesticated animal and explain how animal movement across regions creates lasting benefits.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Names at least two cow breeds not mentioned in the story (e.g., Sahiwal, Red Sindhi, Tharparkar, or any other valid breed identified during the inquiry activity).
States clearly that animals, like plants and ideas, can cross continents and bring lasting benefit to new places.
Makes a connection to the chapter's broader theme — that trade and travel move not just goods but living beings that become part of other societies.

assessment_items.question_text: During the classroom inventory activity, students looked for everyday objects that may have come from other parts of the world. Which of the following items most likely originated outside India, based on what the chapter tells us?

options.label: A
options.text: A bunch of marigolds for a festival

options.label: B
options.text: A mango from a local market

options.label: C
options.text: A yoga mat used at home

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. The marigold originated in Mexico and is the item in this list that came to India from outside. The other three items (jaggery, mango, yoga) originated in India and spread outward. This item tests whether students can distinguish arrivals from departures — the core skill of the inventory activity.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Story 6: The Cows that Went to Brazil!, Web of Life
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe everyday objects in their immediate environment and identify their global origins, demonstrating that daily life is shaped by cross-continental exchange.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student did not retain that jaggery and sugar production originated in India and spread outward — they may have confused the direction of the sugar story.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student did not retain that mangoes are one of the items the chapter identifies as travelling FROM India to other lands.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student did not retain that yoga is India's gift to the world — they may be thinking of the yoga mat as a foreign import rather than the practice itself being Indian in origin.

assessment_items.question_text: In the two-string map activity, you traced things that came TO India and things that went FROM India. Choose one item from each direction — one that came to India and one that went from India — and for each one, explain how it changed the lives of people where it arrived.
expected_elements: Names one item that arrived in India from another country (e.g., chilli from South America, marigold from Mexico, paper from China, rosy starlings from Russia or Mongolia) and explains one way it changed Indian life.

Names one item that went from India to another part of the world (e.g., yoga, sugar or jaggery, rice, mangoes, bananas, Indian cow breeds to Brazil) and explains one way it changed life in the receiving place.
Shows understanding that exchange flows in both directions, with both giver and receiver benefiting.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any chapter-supported item for each direction. The quality of the explanation of impact is the primary assessment target. Regional variation in chosen examples is perfectly acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can organise information about intercontinental exchanges into a two-directional map, distinguishing what arrived in a region from what departed, and draw conclusions about global interconnection.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Names one item that arrived in India from another country (e.g., chilli from South America, marigold from Mexico, paper from China, rosy starlings from Russia or Mongolia) and explains one way it changed Indian life.

Names one item that went from India to another part of the world (e.g., yoga, sugar or jaggery, rice, mangoes, bananas, Indian cow breeds to Brazil) and explains one way it changed life in the receiving place.
Shows understanding that exchange flows in both directions, with both giver and receiver benefiting.

assessment_items.task: The chapter teaches us 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' — the world is one family. Think about what this means for the way you live every day. Write three to five sentences explaining what this idea means to you, and then write one specific thing you will do to care for the Earth. Your response should show that you understand how caring for the Earth and caring for each other are connected.
assessment_items.scaffold: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam means ___. This idea tells me that ___. One way I see this in my daily life is ___. The one thing I will do to care for the Earth is ___, because ___.
format_of_output: Written response of three to five sentences following the scaffold
assessment_items.annotation: The response must show understanding of the idea (not just quote the phrase), connect it to daily life, and name a concrete personal action. A response that only quotes the phrase without explanation does not meet the criterion. Accept any honest and feasible personal action — planting a tree, saving water, not wasting food, reducing plastic — as equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate the meaning of a core social-ethical value in their own words and identify at least one concrete personal action that expresses care for the shared Earth.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can move from a philosophical idea (world as one family) to a personal ethical commitment (concrete Earth-care action), demonstrating that the disposition has been internalised and is not merely a phrase to recall.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold has five slots: meaning of the phrase, what it tells the student about human relationships, one example from daily life, one personal action, and a reason for that action. A strong response fills all five with genuine thought; a weak response fills one or two slots with vague phrases.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: explains the idea in own words (not a quotation), gives a specific daily-life example of mutual care, names a realistic and concrete action with a clear reason linking it to the Earth-as-family idea. Weak: copies the phrase without explaining it, names an action without connecting it to the Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam idea, or gives a vague action ('I will be good to nature').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who prefer expressing this through a short poem or a drawing with a caption may do so — the disposition is the target, not the prose format. A poem that captures mutual care and one action is fully acceptable.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written reflective response with one committed action
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook's 'Let us reflect' tasks explicitly invite written personal commitment, and this format mirrors that invitation while keeping the output observable and assessable in a single sitting.
